canberra.title: Airbus ultra long-range test aircraft sets likely new commercial endurance flight record
canberra.snippet: An Airbus A350-1000ULR airliner designed to fly nonstop from Sydney to London or New York has unofficially broken the record for the long...
canberra.content:
Airbus’ test A350-1000ULR F-WULR touches down in Melbourne on 24 July after a nonstop flight from Toulouse, France. Image: SydSquad Live screenshot.

An Airbus A350-1000ULR airliner designed to fly nonstop from Sydney to London or New York has unofficially broken the record for the longest nonstop flight by a commercial aircraft.

The aircraft – appropriately registered F-WULR and operated by four Airbus test pilots and five flight test engineers – landed in Melbourne at 10:45 on Friday (24 July) after a nonstop 17-hour and 13-minute flight from Airbus’ test facility and factory in Toulouse, France.

After a weekend on the ground in Melbourne, it departed just after 5:00 pm local on Monday (27 July), and took the much longer easterly route back to Toulouse via the Pacific and across North America, Greenland, the Atlantic and UK, and landed in Toulouse after more than 24-hours in the air.

The feat beats by more than an hour the previous 22-hour 45 minutes record set by a Boeing 777-200LR which flew easterly from Hong Kong to London in November 2005. While the record is yet to be ratified by the Guinness Book of Records, the Airbus aircraft appears to have easily surpassed the 11,664 nautical miles (21,601 km) flown by its Boeing rival.

The A350-1000ULR has been designed to a specification set by Qantas for that airline’s ambitious Project Sunrise which it hopes will allow passengers to fly nonstop between Australia’s east coast and London or New York. Currently, Qantas services to London are required to make a fuel stop in Singapore or Perth, while New York services stop in Los Angeles or Auckland.

The ULR – for ultra long range – is the latest variant of the successful large twin-engined airliner. It combines the fuselage of the stretched A350-1000 with a new 20,000-litre integral centre fuel tank designed to provide an additional 1800 km of range for nonstop passenger flights of up to 22 hours.

The first A350 that will be delivered to Qantas was rolled out at Toulouse on 17 June. Photo: Stuart Bailey via Qantas.

The new fuel tank forms part of the aircraft’s structure and its fuel system is different to other models, so the ULR will need to undergo a test program. This program includes maximum braking tests, minimum take-off speed (‘unstick’ or VMU), in-flight handling, and long-range proving flights in order to be certified for passenger service.

The test aircraft is currently the only one flying, making its first flight on 2 June. After flying several shorter test flights around Europe and the UK, the visit to Melbourne and return to Toulouse is its first long-range test.

Rather than being equipped with an airliner interior, the aircraft is fitted with banks of test instrumentation, and water barrels that can be filled to replicate a full load of passengers, luggage, and freight.

The test aircraft will be refurbished at the end of the flight test program and delivered to Qantas as the second or third A350-1000ULR in the fleet. The fact it has been kept in primer or undercoat colours for the flight test campaign has led some enthusiasts – including your writer – to suggest it may appear in a special heritage or First Nations paint scheme when it is delivered.

The first aircraft the airline will take – to be registered VH-OJA in service – was rolled out in Qantas colours at Toulouse without engines on 18 June, and is scheduled for delivery by the end of the year.

In service, the aircraft will feature a low density cabin with 140 Economy class seats in a nine-abreast 3-3-3 configuration, 40 Premium Economy seats in an eight-abreast 2-4-2 layout, 52 Business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, and just six First class ‘suites’.

Early passenger flights will be conducted on short and medium-range routes while Qantas builds up its crews, ground handling, and maintenance processes, with long-haul services due to start in mid-2027.

Qantas is due to take delivery of 12 A350-1000ULRs, as well as 12 standard A350-1000s. It is planned that these new and highly efficient aircraft will replace older A330-300s and the airline’s 10 remaining A380s in service by 2032.

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: You can’t be confident the CFMEU hasn’t tried to influence other procurement decisions, watchdog says
canberra.snippet: The ACT’s Integrity Commissioner says it would be “unreal” to think unions haven’t tried to influence other Terri...
canberra.content:
Integrity Commissioner Michael Adams KC (centre – with the office’s CFO Scott Hickey and CEO Judy Lind) said lobbying was the focus of an ongoing investigation. Photo: Screenshot.

The ACT’s Integrity Commissioner says it would be “unreal” to think unions haven’t tried to influence other Territory procurement processes, but there’s no evidence to suggest they succeeded.

Michael Adams KC was asked during budget estimates about pressure from the CFMEU on procurements in the wake of the Operation Kingfisher report.

When asked by ACT Greens Yerrabi MLA Andrew Braddock whether Canberrans could have confidence similar conduct or influence didn’t occur for other projects, Mr Adams simply responded: “You can’t.”

“If they did it in one case, and they thought it was legitimate, why would you not suppose they attempted the same in other cases?” he answered.

“That doesn’t mean [any other attempt] was always a successful conversation … the point, I think, is [this type of interaction] was seen as everyday, business as usual, and an accepted thing.”

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton more pointedly asked if Mr Adams thought this was the first such attempt by the CFMEU.

“Oh, I don’t think so. That would be unreal,” Mr Adams responded.

Mr Adams explained the issue here was that Manteena was “singled out” by the union to not receive the tender for the Campbell Primary School modernisation project.

“What happened here was the senior members of the [CFMEU] actually sought out the delegate in charge of procurement and told him that he did not wish for Manteena to succeed,” he explained.

“There was actual involvement [by the CFMEU], actual threat … [and now] the threat’s there, isn’t it?

“What happens at the next procurement if the CFMEU is unhappy with you? Nothing has to be said.”

Where to draw the line between presenting interests to political parties and exerting extreme pressure is the focus of a current Integrity Commission investigation into lobbying.

Mr Adams said it was “clear” such communications from all sorts of bodies were happening every day.

“You need to have those communications, but how do you control them to ensure they’re appropriate?” he asked.

Improvements have already been made to the ACT’s procurement processes, given this project was also the focus of an Auditor-General report.

Mr Adams felt further training for public servants was needed about the process, despite work that’s already been done to explain the rules with greater clarity.

“It’s one thing to have it in a document, it’s another thing to actually bring it to people’s active attention,” he said.

He also questioned why the government should be informing interested parties about the identity of tenderers during a procurement process.

As for how long it took for Operation Kingfisher to produce its final report, Mr Adams said it was not purely a resourcing issue.

The Integrity Commission is funded to hire 26.8 full-time equivalent positions.

Mr Adams said the nature of the office’s investigations meant asking how long one would take was like asking how long is a piece of string.

“We start with a reasonable suspicion of corrupt conduct … and we’re looking for where things go,” he explained.

“You have quite a number of false trails that double up, iterative processes, matters that you think aren’t important that six months down the track become important, and vice versa.

“Throwing more resources at it doesn’t actually help because, in the end … [all information has] got to come to one mind.

“It takes the time that it takes.”

Operation Kingfisher, for example, started in March 2021. It examined more than 1.8 million digital records, analysed more than 6500 documents, took evidence from 30 witnesses, and the transcript of evidence of all examinations totalled more than 3827 pages.

For that reason, the public shouldn’t expect firm timelines on the completion of the Commission’s 12 other pending investigations, including the Phillip Pool development.

“Until you actually lift up a rock, you don’t know what’s underneath,” Mr Adams said.

The findings of serious corrupt conduct from Operation Kingfisher have been referred to ACT Policing and the Director of Public Prosecutions.

In light of the Operation Kingfisher findings, Public Service Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith confirmed that Chief Minister Andrew Barr had requested a “quick review” into whether other major procurement processes had been compromised.

“If anybody is aware of any issues of integrity or lack of probity in a procurement process, they should be raising that,” she said.

“People should be reporting and escalating these issues, making public interest disclosures if necessary, and going to the Integrity Commission if it’s a matter of integrity rather than poor process.”

canberra.title: ACT Government faces union campaign against yes vote in pay offer ballot
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government’s latest pay offer to its workforce has hit an obstacle with the main public servants’ union announcing it...
canberra.content:
CPSU ACT regional secretary Maddy Northam warns workers will leave the ACT. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT Government’s latest pay offer to its workforce has hit an obstacle with the main public servants’ union announcing it will campaign against it in the upcoming ballot, including potential strike action.

The CPSU’s rejection of the proposed enterprise agreement comes after it polled its members from 20 to 27 July.

CPSU members were asked if they accepted the ACT Government’s offer and 66 per cent voted no.

The CPSU said its campaign would include meetings with workers, conversations in the workplace and potential industrial action.

CPSU Regional Secretary Maddy Northam said members had comprehensively rejected the ACT Government’s updated pay offer.

The new offer maintains a 9 per cent pay increase in equal instalments over three years, with a twice-yearly increase of 1.5 per cent in July and February.

But it also includes a $600 cost-of-living payment if the ACT’s annual CPI reaches 3.5 per cent or higher, increasing to $1000 if it reaches 4 per cent or higher, as well as expanded entitlements.

Ms Northam said the offer was not up to scratch and members would now be running a vote no campaign and encouraging the government to improve its offer.

“Members have been clear that they will not tolerate another three years of below-inflation pay increases that send their families backwards,” she said.

“Public servants still have to put food on the table and pay the rent.”

Ms Northam indicated that the health system in particular could suffer if there was not a better offer.

She said that if the government did not improve the offer, it ran the risk of highly skilled professionals in the health system leaving the jurisdiction for greener pastures.

“Canberrans can’t afford to lose these workers,” she said.

“The government must step up and back their workforce.”

A government spokesperson said the government would not be improving the offer or delaying the vote.

The updated offer was a third and genuine effort to reach a fair and balanced agreement that recognised employees’ important work while ensuring the long-term sustainability of the ACT’s finances.

“We acknowledge and respect the outcome of the CPSU’s member survey. The offer will now go to a formal ballot,” the spokesperson said.

While a majority of CPSU members had rejected the offer, the government had been encouraged by several other unions to put it to a vote.

“We are committed to finalising an agreement so employees can receive the benefits of the proposed package as soon as possible,” the spokesperson said.

“We will continue to engage with employees in good faith and now await the ballot outcome.”

Public servants will receive a copy of the proposed agreement on 12 August to assess ahead of the ballot, which will open on 26 August and conclude at 4 pm on 8 September.

canberra.title: ‘Honour the trust’: Man who used counterfeit notes in clubs avoids jail sentence upon release
canberra.snippet: The sight of a “glimmer of hope” in a man has seen him handed a kind of deferred sentence. Bradley James Takkenberg faced the...
canberra.content:
Bradley James Takkenberg, of Ngunnawal, will return to court for sentencing in December. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The sight of a “glimmer of hope” in a man has seen him handed a kind of deferred sentence.

Bradley James Takkenberg faced the ACT Galambany Court for sentencing on charges of minor theft, unlawful possession of stolen property and multiple counts of obtaining property by deception.

On Tuesday (28 July), Magistrate Jane Campbell ultimately handed Takkenberg a Griffiths remand.

This is a sentencing option that will see his immediate release, with sentencing deferred while he undergoes rehabilitation.

She said the outcome came in light of “a glimmer of hope” that the Elders saw in him and urged him to “honour the trust” they placed in him.

“Bradley, when people are on a deferred sentence or a Griffiths remand, it’s important that you comply … The consequences [with failing to do so] are going to be that you go into full-time custody.”

During an earlier appearance last Thursday (23 July), he repeatedly told the Elders he was committed to turning his life around.

He said he had started taking drugs when he was young and outlined childhood experiences of trauma and violence.

“I’m willing to do the hard work, I really am,” he said.

When asked about his youth, Takkenberg said he was “a pretty lost boy growing up” and “didn’t have a role model [to act as a] father figure”.

He said he was willing to speak with a counsellor and also discussed various rehabilitative services in the region that he could attend with the Elders.

He also said he wanted to be “more connected to my culture” and was willing to address “underlying issues” affecting his relationship with his son.

“I’m nearly 30 now … I’ve got my son now … I’m really recognising that drugs and alcohol, especially when you’ve got kids, is not good.”

Takkenberg’s defence lawyer said his client’s drug use and other “maladaptive coping strategies” followed his history of trauma.

“He’s not a lost cause,” he said.

He pointed to the then-28-year-old’s offending from November 2025 – when Takkenberg used counterfeit notes at two clubs before a stash of fake cash was found at his home – and said the fake notes were of poor quality and missing key security features.

He described the offending as being “very unsophisticated” and “not well-thought out, well-planned” behaviour.

Takkenberg’s lawyer suggested a deferred sentence and also sought a discount of 20 to 25 per cent to his client’s sentence.

But prosecutor Harry Wagner said a 15 per cent discount would be appropriate and described that November 2025 offending as being “premeditated” and carried out “for the purpose of deceiving others”.

He also said past offending while on parole raised questions about Takkenberg’s future compliance with another community-based sentence.

Magistrate Campbell listed his sentence for 10 December, meaning he will return to court then.

“The Elders very much were of the view that you’ve spent a considerable amount of time already in custody,” she told Takkenberg.

“We hope that’s going to be a motivator for you and with a Griffith remand, I set certain expectations for you over the period of time that you’re out in the community.”

Under the conditions of his release, Takkenberg will need to enter a rehabilitation program by a set date and tell the court if he fails to complete a program for any reason.

“That can be something for you to decide,” she said of the specific program he chooses.

While on bail, Takkenberg will also need to live at a Ngunnawal address, not access online marketplaces, follow an overnight curfew and not drink alcohol or use any illegal drugs.

The court heard his relationship with his then-partner, and co-accused, is finished. She is set to be sentenced next month.

canberra.title: ACTU secretary and president announce joint resignations
canberra.snippet: Praise has poured in from across the political divide for the Australian Council of Trade Union’s leadership team of president Michele O&...
canberra.content:
ACTU Secretary Sally McManus and ACTU President Michele O’Neil have announced their resignations. Image: Screenshot.

Praise has poured in from across the political divide for the Australian Council of Trade Union’s leadership team of president Michele O’Neil and secretary Sally McManus, who have both announced surprise resignations.

The peak union body issued a statement Tuesday morning (28 July) saying the pair were stepping down to bring renewal to the movement and make way for a new generation of union leaders.

The pair have claimed extensive new rights have been won for working Australians, and the union movement has grown under their lead, but say the time is right to transition to a new leadership team.

“As the ACTU President, I’ve been proud to be part of a team leading a movement determined to win new rights for working people that make a real difference in the lives of workers and their families,” Ms O’Neil said.

“Every win we have achieved together has not been because of individuals, but come as a result of workers standing together.

“When I was elected president, the challenge was clear: workers’ rights were under attack, jobs and industries were being lost, insecure work was on the rise.

“Having the opportunity with our movement to campaign for and win change has been the honour of my life.”

Ms O’Neill said she and Ms McManus had decided to announce their decisions together and to stagger their leaving times.

She will stay on as ACTU President until sometime before the end of the year to support the transition to the new leadership team.

The secretary will step down at the end of August.

“I am proud of our movement’s achievements, and it has been an honour to serve the union movement and working people as the Secretary of the ACTU for nearly a decade,” Ms McManus said.

“This is the right time to make way for new leadership to take our movement forward and to face new challenges.

“When I took on this role, workers’ rights were under attack and workplace laws desperately needed fixing. I wanted to be part of turning that around … It is an absolute privilege representing working people, and I’ve given it my all. Now I look forward to supporting new leaders stepping up.”

Ms McManus and Ms O’Neil were elected to the ACTU leadership in 2017 and 2018 respectively and are the longest-serving ACTU leadership team since 1969.

Anthony Albanese issued a statement praising the union leaders.

The Prime Minister said working families were in a stronger financial position today than they would otherwise be because of the “tireless advocacy and strong leadership” of Ms McManus and Ms O’Neil.

“Sally and Michele secured incredible successes for working people in their eight years together leading Australia’s union movement – the first all-female leadership team in the Australian Council of Trade Unions’ 99-year history,” Mr Albanese said.

“It is fitting that Sally and Michele announce they’re stepping down from their respective positions at a time when there have been significant wage increases in critical and long-undervalued sectors, the gender pay gap is at a record low and union membership is growing for the first time in decades.

“Personally, I will miss the friendship and support these two giants of the labour movement have offered me over many years, but especially since I became Labor Leader in 2019 and then Prime Minister in 2022.

“I wish both Sally and Michele all the very best in wherever their next paths lead and look forward to working with the new leadership team of the ACTU once they’re in place.”

Employment and Workplace Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth said the pair “have left a formidable legacy” in delivering for working Australians.

“I thank them for their exceptional leadership of the ACTU,” she said.

“Through a combined 17 years of action as secretary and president, McManus and O’Neil were trailblazers who made daily life better for millions of Australians.”

The Greens also praised the pair for their advocacy.

Greens leader Larissa Waters described them as “strong voices for workers” who both led the union movement with courage, principle and compassion.

“They have been a powerful duo for almost a decade, and I’m so proud to have had two strong women leading the union movement,” Senator Waters said.

“The Greens are proud to have worked alongside the ACTU to stop governments putting the interests of big corporations ahead of people’s rights at work.”

Even Nationals leader Matt Canavan wished both women well.

“I’ve never been someone who’s been anti-union,” Senator Canavan said.

“I’ve worked with many unions over the time to protect workers’ jobs and rights.

“I do find the ACTU, though, has generally found itself more focused on activist campaigns rather than those workers’ rights.”

The ACTU’s union affiliates will decide on the next leadership team, initially with the ACTU Executive filling the casual vacancies and then through an election at next year’s Congress.

australia.title: Guardian Essential poll: Angus Taylor’s approval rating crashes and One Nation support plateaus
australia.snippet: Survey also shows Australians rounding on the government over its handling of inflation and the cost of living crisis Get our breaking ne...
australia.content:
One Nation’s primary vote has plateaued and Angus Taylor’s approval rating has crashed, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll.

But it is not all smooth sailing for Labor with Australians rubbishing the government’s handling of the inflation and cost of living crisis.

Australians have also shown their reluctance to embrace new AI datacentres, with less than a third saying they’d be happy to have a facility in their local area and sharing concerns about energy demands, water supply, environmental impacts and noise.

The Guardian Essential poll, of 1,060 voters last week, found One Nation’s popularity was continuing to level off, attracting a 25% primary vote, down one point from June’s poll. Meanwhile while Labor’s indicative primary vote ticked up one point to 31% and the Coalition’s vote dropped further, down another point to 22%.

All those movements are within the poll’s margin of error, but it is the second consecutive Essential poll where One Nation’s primary vote has dropped since reaching a high of 28% in May. The populist right-wing party has dipped back to where it was in April. It comes after weeks of scrutiny over Pauline Hanson’s European trip, her interview with Tommy Robinson, and comments about domestic violence and immigration policy.

Struggling for political oxygen and attention amidst One Nation’s rise, the opposition leader has seen his own approval ratings plummet in the last month. In June, 36% of people approved of Taylor’s job performance and 37% disapproved, for a net approval of minus-1; but this month’s poll has seen his approvals drop three points and his disapprovals increase by seven points, for a new net approval of minus-12.

Taylor’s approval rating has crashed 16 points among men and four points among women, as well as by 20 points among people aged 35-54 and 13 points among those aged 18-34.

Anthony Albanese’s approval rating ticked up one point to minus-14, with 38% approving and 52% disapproving of his performance as prime minister. It’s the fourth straight month in which more than half of voters have disapproved of his performance.

Respondents to the poll also rejected Labor’s handling of the inflation and cost of living crisis, with a decisive 64% rating the government’s performance as poor; while just 16% of Australians rated it as good.

Nearly 80% of voters said cost of living and inflation was one of the most important issues to them, far and away the most-cited issue among respondents. Next most-cited was Medicare and health (50%), crime (42%) and immigration (35%).

But only 39% of voters rated the Labor government’s performance on Medicare and health as good, with 30% saying poor; on crime, 22% rated Labor as good and 50% as poor, while 24% rated Labor as good on immigration and another 50% as poor.

“Cost of living remains the stand-out issue for voters and the government’s handling of inflation is being rated down,” the executive director of Essential Media, Peter Lewis, said.

On managing technology and AI, the subject of a major speech by Albanese earlier this month, 29% rated Labor’s performance as good and 30% as poor.

The Essential report found only 28% of voters would support a new datacentre being built in their area, with 37% against. Men (34% support and 34% oppose) were far more supportive of new datacentres than women (22% support and 39% oppose).

Asked about their reservations about datacentre development, 61% raised concerns about impact on energy demand and power prices, and another 44% were worried about water supply.

Environmental impacts and noise were raised by 41% of voters, while 39% had general concerns about the growth of AI generally.

Albanese this month announced plans to more strongly regulate datacentres and AI, particularly setting rules for power and water use, and building social license for the construction of facilities.

australia.title: Royal commission into Victorian construction sector could boost Labor’s chances at state election, expert says
australia.snippet: Commission promised by new premier would be an ‘important signal’ for voters that the government was acting on alleged corruption Get our...
australia.content:
Victorian voters heading to the polls will probably get a taste of the evidence heard by a royal commission – including how taxpayer funds were used on Big Build projects – but it could actually help Labor’s standing, an integrity expert says.

William Partlett, an associate professor of law and a fellow at the Centre for Public Integrity, said the commission promised by the new premier, Ben Carroll, would be an “important signal” for voters that the government was taking action.

Shortly after being sworn in on Tuesday, Carroll said the creation of a royal commission into the construction sector would be his “first action” as premier. This follows sustained pressure to investigate alleged corruption on the government’s Big Build infrastructure projects.

Carroll said the commission’s terms of reference would be “exhaustive”, and it would be established “as soon as possible”, suggesting it could hold hearings before November’s state election.

“Whether it’s the top-tier companies, whether it’s subcontractors, whether it’s businesses or unions, these terms of reference will be thorough,” the premier said.

Carroll also said a special prosecutor would be appointed to work in parallel to the royal commission, and that the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission will be bolstered with follow-the-money powers.

It comes after his predecessor, Jacinta Allan, had resisted calls for a royal commission into allegations that organised crime figures and bikie gangs infiltrated major infrastructure projects, including the Big Build.

Partlett told Guardian Australia the decision to hold a royal commission was not surprising, given the pressure the former premier was under from the Labor caucus over the issue.

“In some ways it was probably the downfall of [Allan] in her failure to call that because it did seem that many wanted that to be called,” Partlett said.

The Big Build is the state’s infrastructure program that has, since 2015, given about $109bn in public money for more than 180 projects, including the Metro Tunnel, level crossing removals and the Suburban Rail Loop.

Many of the projects had suffered cost blowouts, which Allan had previously said was due to inflation, supply chain disruptions and rising labour costs. Her claims came in response to reporting by the Age that money from the projects was being paid to gangland figures, and alleged union corruption was adding premiums of up to 30% to major project budgets.

Allan later acknowledged there had been criminality in the projects but said it was best for police to investigate any allegations of wrongdoing.

A report by the Centre for Public Integrity’s director, Geoffrey Watson SC, tabled during a Queensland inquiry into the CFMEU, found that “the flood of government money” had made the Big Build “ripe for corruption”.

That included “ad hoc corruption on the part of former organisers and delegates” as well as “a more organised or systemic corruption involving collaboration by some elements in the CFMEU with outlaw motorcycle gangs and other crime outfits,” Watson wrote.

The report stated a labourer’s job on the Big Build was so lucrative that a market was allegedly created where corrupt organisers and delegates bought and sold the jobs, and alleged the government “knew and had a duty to know” about wrongdoing but chose to do “nothing about it”.

Partlett said the terms of reference for the commission need to be “as broad as they can be” to include private organisations, the unions, institutions and government officials. The commission should also use its coercive powers to get to the bottom of the allegations in an open and transparent way, he said.

He said it was important that the commission begin sooner rather than later, and would have some potential impact on the election.

“The fact that the Labor party now is showing that it has interest in tackling these issues is an important signal … they are willing to accept something has gone wrong.”

Partlett said Labor getting in before the election allows them to set the terms of reference, and no one in the integrity sector would like to see it turn into “a demonisation of unions”.

“They can make it an inquiry into the construction sector that is done in a responsible way. It doesn’t demonise the unions, but then at the same time tries to understand what went wrong here.”

australia.title: Anger at Labor as Rex Patrick faces potential six-figure legal fee if he loses Aukus documents battle
australia.snippet: Australian government insists legal costs should be paid by former senator as FoI fight escalates Get our breaking news email , free app ...
australia.content:
The government will insist Rex Patrick pays up to $150,000 to cover its legal costs if he loses a fight to access documents about the Aukus agreement, escalating a battle in which several crossbench MPs have swung behind the former senator.

The transparency campaigner has used freedom of information laws to seek details on where nuclear waste from the submarine fleet will be stored, and won an administrative appeal on the matter in May.

But the Department of Industry, Science and Resources has appealed the matter to the federal court, seeking the decision be overturned and an order for Patrick to pay the government’s legal costs if he loses.

Politicians including Jacqui Lambie and Pauline Hanson have lashed the decision, warning it is a breach of rules requiring the government to act as a model litigant.

They, along with unions and transparency groups, have made appeals to the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, but have been rebuffed.

According to documents seen by Guardian Australia, Rowland last week said the government could rightly insist on Patrick being required to pay costs if he loses, acting “firmly and properly” to protect its interests.

Rowland wrote to a group of crossbenchers – including independents Helen Haines, David Pocock and the Greens’ David Shoebridge – saying the industry department was responsible for conduct of the case.

The department does not accept the model litigant rules prevent it from seeking costs from Patrick. Previous legal fights have seen fees of much as $150,000.

Lambie has accused Rowland of “behaving like a Labor stooge”.

“The government is sending a very clear message to people: stop when we say you can’t have information under FoI, or we’ll take you to court and you could lose all your savings … and maybe your house,” she said.

“I cannot believe the attorney general has handballed what is a whole-of-government principle issue to the secretary of a single department. The attorney is behaving like a Labor stooge, and either doesn’t have any leadership within her or doesn’t care. So which one is it?

“This issue is not going to just go away.”

Organisations including the Media Entertainment & Arts Alliance, the Grata Fund, the Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom and Australian Democracy Network have all called on the government to stop the legal challenge.

Tosca Lloyd, a Whistleblower Justice Fund campaigner, said the risk of a six-figure legal bill would limit ordinary use of FoI rules.

“This chilling effect is neither hypothetical nor unintentional,” she said.

“Public interest journalism depends on the FoI system. Investigative reporters – especially those at smaller and independent outlets – use it constantly to uncover stories the public has a right to know.

“If the cost of challenging a bad government decision is federal court litigation, most newsrooms simply won’t take that risk. The stories then won’t get told. That’s a loss for all of us.”

Bill Browne, the Australia Institute’s Democracy & Accountability program director, said departments and ministers should not fight FoI applicants.

“The Albanese government already tried to restrict Australians’ right to access government information, and was rebuffed by the Senate. This looks like another attempt to raise the cost of scrutinising the government.”

Patrick said legal precedent dating back to a 1912 high court decision showed a “standard of fair play” should be observed by governments.

“I have some experience in courtrooms and have asked the court to ensure fairness from government and that these laws will be decided with competent barristers arguing different sides of the secrecy/transparency questions before it,” he said.

“I can just hope that the courts will address the misguided sense of fairness and proper process exhibited by the attorney general.”

A spokesperson for Rowland declined to comment, referring questions to the department.

australia.title: Angus Taylor has inadvertently taken centre stage in an Icac hearing – and the fallout could be profound
australia.snippet: If the opposition leader was funding one side of a vicious factional war, it would be hard for many in the party to stomach Get our break...
australia.content:
Independent Commission against Corruption inquiries have an uncanny tendency to sprawl in unexpected directions.

Just ask former New South Wales premier, Gladys Berejiklian, who was caught on tape with her secret boyfriend, former NSW MP Daryl Maguire, during an investigation into his dealings with developers. Or former premier Barry O’Farrell, who was tripped up over a bottle of Penfolds Grange during an inquiry into state water contracts.

In the Icac hearing on Tuesday into allegations of corruption against people associated with the NSW Liberal party, the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, took centre stage – even though he was hundreds of kilometres away in Rockhampton. He is not accused of wrongdoing.

The bombshell came in a group chat of young Liberal power brokers known as “Reformers” who are at the centre of Icac’s Operation Rosny, an investigation into alleged breaches of the NSW Electoral Funding Act.

The secretive Reformers group were a sub-faction of the right of the NSW Liberals who were intent on restoring conservative values to the party. The Icac is looking at alleged undisclosed donations made by the fugitive developer Jean Nassif and others that were used to fund the Reformers’ efforts to recruit members and take over branches.

Taylor surfaced in a message from Dallas McInerney, head of the Catholic Schools Association NSW and supporter of the Reformers, which was shared with the group in March 2021. In the message McInerney allegedly said he planned to “to shake down Angus for $10,000” while at a meeting in Canberra.

On Tuesday, a former NSW Liberal parliamentary staffer and associate of the Reformers, Dylan Whitelaw, who is not named in Icac’s allegations, gave evidence. He was shown a message sent to the group in which he allegedly wrote “Dallas has told me he got the commitment from Angus the 15k injection plus a 3k monthly donation!” Whitelaw said he did not recall sending the message, nor did he recall Taylor making a financial contribution to the Reformers.

We don’t know whether Taylor actually made the payments – and even if he did, there’s a question over whether they were covered by NSW’s political donations laws. A statement issued after Taylor was named at Icac did not deny the payments or address them directly.

“The Leader is not a party to the matters before the commission, nor has he been approached,” a spokesperson for Taylor said in a statement. “Donations and fundraising activities are declared in accordance with the rules and are a matter for the Party.”

The implications, if these payments were made, though, could be profound.

For a start, there is a question as to whether these are undeclared political donations or in breach of the donation caps in NSW’s Electoral Funding Act.

This would be serious for the leader of a major political party.

But there is also the internal political fallout. The Reformers were set up to demolish the Centre Right faction and wrest control of the NSW party from the Moderates.

If it was proven that their leader was funding one side of a vicious factional war, it would be hard for many in the party to stomach.

Taylor does not appear as a donor on the NSW donation disclosure register in 2020-2021, 2021-22 or 2022-23. He is listed on the federal donations register as having made only one $1,500 donation in 2010 – to Malcolm Turnbull’s campaign.

Icac is also investigating other alleged donors to the Reformers, including Nassif, former hotelier Michael O’Hara, and Catholic Schools NSW. McInerney has stood down as Catholic Schools NSW CEO and is expected to give evidence later in the inquiry.

Nassif allegedly paid a total of $2m to Reformers members Christian Ellis, Charles Perrottet and Jeremy Greenwood. O’Hara paid $165,000 and Catholic Schools NSW donated over $250,000.

Some of these funds were allegedly paid under sham arrangements to public relations firms controlled by Ellis and Greenwood.

Most of Tuesday was spent hearing evidence from Whitelaw, who joined the Liberals when he left school and who was vice-president of the Mittagong branch of the Liberal party. He soon fell into the orbit of the conservative Reformers.

In 2019 he went to work for Catholic Schools NSW and later for Ellis’s public relations firm, Beckington, again on Reformer work.

His evidence revealed how Catholic Schools NSW, a registered charity, was used to employ young men in the Reformers.

The organisation is responsible for funding Catholic schools in NSW and administers nearly $4bn in state and federal grants for the sector.

The allegations will now turn attention to whether there are breaches of charities laws and politicisation of a major education funding body.

Whitelaw was employed by Catholic Schools NSW as a data processor, a junior role, but told the commission he spent much of his time on Reformers work, which included organising events and recruiting like-minded conservative members in the Wollondilly area.

Robert Assaf, a key member of the Reformers, was also employed at Catholic Schools. Cecile Piat, Ellis’ wife, was employed as a secretary.

“Rob did very little Catholic Schools work,” Whitelaw said. “It was a running joke between me and Rob,” he said, adding that his “guess” was Assaf spent 60% of his time on Reformer work and 40% on “his real job.”

There is a live issue, still to be addressed by Icac, as to whether the contributions to the Reformers were caught by the NSW political donations laws.

The group was doing political work – it was recruiting conservatives to branches, trying to take control of the Liberal party administrative structure and attempting to influence policy, but it had no formal status within the Liberal party.

O’Hara, the hotelier and former business partner of right power broker and MP Damien Tudehope, took issue with whether the payments he made to the Reformers were political donations.

The Reformers were not registered as a political party, or a third-party entity, raising questions about how far the Electoral Funding Act reaches to require disclosure of donations to entities outside the formal party structure.

Counsel assisting the inquiry, Peggy Dwyer SC spent considerable time seeking to establish that O’Hara knew the Reformers were recruiting conservatives to branches, and that the objective was to take over branches from the Moderates.

But O’Hara became disillusioned by 2022 and pulled his funding. In his last conversation with the Reformers, he told Jean Claude Perrottet he would only pay the most recent invoices, adding: “I may as well support the Greens or Teals, as Dominic [Perrottet] was rolled on so many issues instead of prosecuting the principles I believed he stood for.”

australia.title: Banks charged mortgage holders $55m in extra interest after offset account errors, Asic finds
australia.snippet: Australian banks ‘not getting the basics right’, regulator says after review of more than 200,000 home loans Get our breaking news email ...
australia.content:
Asic has accused banks of “not getting the basics right”, after the regulator found faulty mortgage offset accounts meant borrowers were being overcharged tens of millions of dollars in extra interest payments.

In a new report, the Australian Securities and Investment Commission showed lenders repaid $55m to hundreds of thousands of customers over two years for offset failures, and warned this figure would climb higher as remediation continued.

The amount of savings Australians hold in these popular accounts has ballooned to nearly $350bn in recent years. The money is supposed to be offset against the outstanding loan value, reducing the interest payable.

A borrower with an outstanding loan of $100,000 and $20,000 in a properly linked mortgage offset account, for example, should only be paying interest on $80,000.

Asic’s review of more than 200,000 home loans from eight banks unearthed poor practices by lenders.

In one case, a bank accidentally unlinked a customer’s offset account when processing a change to their mortgage. That went undetected until the customer noticed their higher repayments and complained.

In just one month, the customer had paid more than $3,500 in additional interest “as a direct result of the offset account not being linked”, the report found.

Some banks couldn’t readily identify whether the customer had even requested an offset account – a finding which suggested the problem could be even more widespread than initially thought.

Sarah Court, the Asic chair, said “some banks are not getting the basics right”.

“When offset accounts don’t operate correctly, the harm can be hidden. Loan repayments stay the same, while customers unknowingly pay more interest and take longer to repay their loan.”

That represented a double blow to customers who lose the promised interest savings, but also the opportunity to have used that money elsewhere, Court said.

Of the 204,000 home loans, Asic found issues with hundreds of mortgage offset accounts. Simon Birmingham, the CEO of the Australian Banking Association, said this meant that “in more than 99% of cases banks were found to manage them correctly”.

“As the report states, banks have already taken action to compensate the small number of customers where those banks identified errors, often manual errors,” Birmingham said.

Among Asic’s key concerns were that banks had failed to compensate customers and were slow to fix issues, and that it was hard for customers to identify when their offset was not operating as intended.

“In some cases, offset failures went undetected until Asic started asking questions. That should concern every bank offering offset accounts,” Court said.

Meg Dalling, an assistant director at the Consumer Action Law Centre, said “people sign up for mortgage offset accounts with the promise of substantial interest savings – banks must deliver on these promises”.

The multiple failures identified by Asic in its review meant it took longer to pay off a loan, Dalling said.

“This is unacceptable in a cost-of-living crisis – the community expects better from their bank.”

Sally Tindall, the director of data insights at Canstar, said she was “alarmed” by Asic’s findings.

“It is disappointing. People with a mortgage are focused on making their monthly repayment and keeping their heads above water. They don’t have time to be double-checking their bank, and nor should they.”

world.title: Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger
world.snippet: Government move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutrition Uganda has launched emergen...
world.content:
Uganda has launched emergency food relief distribution after at least 19 deaths from hunger were reported in an area of prolonged drought in the east of the country.

A crisis has been building in the Karamoja region of Uganda as crops have failed without the season’s expected rains, leaving the region’s 1.5 million people facing acute food shortages and rising malnutrition.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (Fews Net), a global mapping network designed to raise the alert on food security, reported the situation had deteriorated to a crisis across Karamoja.

In the first large-scale operation of its kind organised by the Ugandan government after the funding void left by aid cuts, authorities announced plans to distribute 9,400 tonnes of relief food over the next two months. The supplies were procured using a 45bn-shilling (£9m) emergency funding allocation, approved by parliament.

Sam Engola, minister for disaster preparedness and refugees, launched the aid distribution efforts at a primary school in Lodiko sub-county in Kaabong district on Wednesday.

“The president does not want to hear of anyone in Karamoja dying of hunger. I am here to supervise the distribution of this food to the end. I will ensure that everyone receives food. No one will be left behind,” Engola said.

Karamoja is experiencing its most severe dry spell in years. Farmers have lost crops since the last meaningful rainfall was recorded in April – the beginning of the planting season.

Angelina Nakiru, a 21-year-old mother of two in Rupa, about 5 miles from Moroto town in Karamoja, said she was struggling to feed her children after all her crops failed. Now she goes early each morning to join other women at a small-scale grinding mill where machines are used to crush rock into powder to wash out gold-bearing ore. The pay is meagre.

“The work is dusty and exhausting, but it is the only way I can earn money to buy a cup of maize and beans to feed the children,” Nakiru said.

“If I don’t, the children will sleep hungry. Other days when I fail to get the meagre income from the mill, we go to bed on empty stomachs,” she said.

“The situation is terrible. People are starving and dying due to hunger. The government must come to the rescue of the people.”

Health facilities report treating hundreds of children for severe malnutrition. A nutrition report published in June found nearly half of the population in Karamoja’s Kaabong and Kotido districts in a crisis situation.

Experts attribute the region’s recurring food insecurity and vulnerability to climate crisis shocks, environmental degradation such as deforestation and overgrazing, as well as poverty and low agricultural productivity.

In 2022, a devastating hunger crisis claimed more than 2,200 lives, according to figures from Uganda’s human rights commission body.

While emergency food aid is expected to provide short-term relief, the government said it remained committed to implementing long-term remedial measures with the recently approved Karamoja regional development plan, which is intended to strengthen communities’ resilience to drought.

John Baptist Lokii, minister for Karamoja, said: “The government will provide drought-resistant, disease-resistant and early-maturing seeds ahead of the next planting season.”

Agnes Kirabo, executive director of Uganda’s Food Rights Alliance (FRA), said the government was taking the lead on distribution as a necessity as much as a policy choice as the landscape of humanitarian aid had changed dramatically.

Following significant funding cuts, most notably from USAID, which previously had an annual budget of about $42.8bn (£32.bn), agencies such as the World Food Programme (WFP) have been forced to drastically scale back their aid.

In Uganda, the WFP has phased out food assistance for 63% of the refugee population, cutting off more than 1 million people from aid, and reducing rations to just 663,000 recipients.

“This transition should not be viewed solely as a reaction to aid cuts, but also as a positive shift towards nationally owned, sustainable development. Government leadership is a constructive move, provided it is part of a long-term strategy to establish durable national systems,” said Kirabo.

“Emergency food distribution is a life-saving measure, not a permanent solution. To break this cycle, we must address the root causes of food insecurity through structural reforms.”

The FRA, Kirabo said, wanted access to food to be made a fundamental human right and the government to turn its attention to water infrastructure and climate resilience. “Karamoja possesses adequate rainfall and water routes to achieve food self-sufficiency, but requires the political will to strategically invest in water infrastructure for production,” she said.

“Ultimately, the Karamoja hunger crisis is a governance crisis. The government’s leadership in this emergency is welcome, but it must be matched by the political will to implement the systemic changes required to permanently protect the people of Karamoja and Uganda from predictable, preventable hunger.”

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report

world.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers
world.snippet: September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences The British army has been f...
world.content:
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.

While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.

According to the Kenyan news outlet the Daily Nation, the dispute centres on which cases Kenya will retain primary jurisdiction over, while the amount of money Britain pays Kenya to host the training camp has also been a sticking point.

The chair of the Kenyan national assembly’s defence, intelligence and foreign relations committee, Nelson Koech, said the two governments were “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues”.

As a result of the Kenyan government’s decision, a planned exercise involving the 1st Battalion the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, which was due to begin in September, has been cancelled.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The UK highly values its relationship with Kenya, which is underpinned by mutual benefit, respect and cooperation. The UK-Kenya Defence Partnership is one of the great strengths of our relationship. Our joint training and operations with the Kenyan Defence Forces are keeping both Kenyan and British people safe.

“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming. As a result, the planned training will now be conducted at an alternative location outside Kenya.”

Kenya also benefits from training of its own armed forces at BATUK, the British army base near Nanyuki, and the presence of British troops is valuable for the economy.

The MoD spokesperson added: “We recognise the disappointment this decision will cause for those who would have benefited from the economic activity generated by the exercise.”

They said the UK government remained “committed to our defence partnership with Kenya”, adding that the UK would “continue to engage closely with the Kenyan government to support the resumption of training in-country at the earliest appropriate opportunity”.

However, there has been sustained pressure from Kenyan people opposed to the British army’s continued presence. Last year, a report to the Kenyan parliament into the base alleged human rights violations, environmental destruction and sexual abuse by British soldiers.

The most high-profile case linked to the base is the death of Agnes Wanjiru, in which a British soldier has been charged with murder. Kenya has retained jurisdiction in the case and an extradition hearing is due to take place in November. Robert Purkiss denies the single charge of murder.

Legal proceedings had stalled since Wanjiru’s death in 2012, but advanced under John Healey’s tenure as defence secretary. As shadow defence secretary, he had called on the previous government to do more to progress the case.

Koech said the committee had called for “stronger accountability measures, including jurisdiction over serious offences, enhanced protection for local communities, and implementation of recommendations arising from the BATUK inquiry”.

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.
